name: Lao kingdoms (Luang Prabang, Vientiane, Champasak)
summary: The three kingdoms that formed when Lan Xang split in 1707; they paid tribute to Siam, and Vientiane was destroyed after King Anouvong’s revolt (1826–28). France took them over in 1893.

location.value: Present-day Laos along the Mekong, which formed the kingdom's political and economic artery. Lan Xang split in 1707 into Luang Prabang and Vientiane; Champasak emerged in 1713. The page does not tie it to north-east Thailand.

terrain.value: Mountains and plateaus around the Mekong valley, with fertile river plains near Vientiane.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: wet summers, dry and cooler winters.

resources.value: Rice, forest products (cardamom, benzoin, ivory) and river fish.

disasters.value: Floods on the Mekong and wars that emptied towns.

population.value: The page gives army sizes but no population figures.

urbanisation.value: Royal towns of Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak, with temples and markets.

migration.value: After 1828 Siam moved tens of thousands of Lao people to the Khorat plateau (north-east Thailand).

economicBase.value: Glutinous rice and forest timber, with trade in elephants, ivory, benzoin, lac, cardamom, beeswax and deer skins. Siam profited from much of this trade, and Chinese merchants traded at Vieng Khuk.

tradeRoutes.value: Mekong river trade and caravans to Yunnan and Siam.

wealth.value: Modest, with royal wealth from tribute and forest products.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver and tribute in kind; corvée labour.

inequality.value: Royalty and nobles above farmers; hill peoples treated as inferior; some slavery.

governmentType.value: Luang Phrabang formed in 1707 from the split of Lan Xang, was an absolute monarchy and a vassal of Siam (1778–1893 in the infobox); the French protectorate was established after the Franco-Siamese conflict of 13 July to 3 October 1893, with the royal family staying in Luang Prabang with reduced power. The page does not cover Vientiane or Champasak.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang (checked 13 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Fa Ngum (crowned 1353); Setthathirath, who moved the capital to Vientiane in 1560. Britannica dates the capital move from Luang Prabang to Vientiane to 1563, not 1560.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Lan Xang (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Lan Xang (checked 15 Nov 2026) (it names Fa Ngum as founder, with Khmer help)

succession.value: Royal families, often with Siamese approval.

institutions.value: Courts with noble officials (chao); the Buddhist monkhood.

stability.value: Weak after 1779; Vientiane was destroyed in 1828.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between Luang Prabang and Vientiane.

majorWars.value: A Siamese invasion was defeated at Sala Kham in 1540; Vientiane fell to Bayinnaung’s Burmese forces in 1574.

territoryChange.value: Siam took the Emerald Buddha to Bangkok (1779) and annexed the west bank of the Mekong.

alliancesRivals.value: Siam and Vietnam as overlords; rivals of each other.

scienceEducation.value: Temple schools taught reading, and palm-leaf manuscripts preserved Buddhist texts.

openness.value: Open to river trade along the Mekong.

communicationTransport.value: River boats on the Mekong; elephants and footpaths.

religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang (checked 13 Nov 2026)

languageWriting.value: Lao in its own script; Tai Tham for religious texts.

artsArchitecture.value: Temples with sweeping roofs such as Wat Xieng Thong (1560) and That Luang.

socialStructure.value: Royal family, nobles, monks, villagers and hill peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: Lao Buddhist identity inherited from Lan Xang.

dailyLife.value: Sticky rice, fish and herbs; houses on stilts.

neighbours.value: Siam, Vietnam, Burma, the Shan states and Cambodia.

ideasReligions.value: Theravada Buddhist kingship shaped the court and society.

riseSignals.value: Lan Xang founded in 1353 by Fa Ngum, crowned that year; capital Luang Prabang (1353–1560).

peakPeriod.value: Lan Xang's height was under Setthathirath, and Sourigna Vongsa (1637–94) ruled through 57 years of peace. Anouvong's revolt of 1826–29 failed and Vientiane was destroyed.

declineSignals.value: The destruction of Vientiane in 1828 after Anouvong’s revolt.

outcome.value: Lan Xang was divided in 1707 into the kingdoms of Luang Prabang and Vientiane; the article gives Champasak as emerging in 1713.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Lan Xang (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Lan Xang (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica says only that Lan Xang split in the 18th century into Vientiane and Luang Prabang; it gives no 1707 date and does not name Champasak)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
